core: Why tourism is not a single industry in standard national accounts, and how a Travel and Tourism Satellite Account (TTSA/TSA) measures its contribution by reallocating visitor spending across industries
Direct vs. indirect vs. induced effects of visitor spending
The tourism multiplier and why estimates vary (method, region, leakage)
Economic leakage: money that leaves the local economy through imports, non-local ownership, taxes, and savings
Tourism as an export and its place in the balance of payments
Costs and limits: seasonality, low wages, over-dependence
supporting: Dated U.S. figures from BEA TTSA (GDP share, direct employment, indirect ratios)
A worked multiplier example using real NPS/USGS Visitor Spending Effects figures, clearly labeled illustrative
outOfScope: The tourism-system model / Leiper / definitions of tourist/visitor (owned by Tourism Systems)
Destination marketing strategy (owned by Destination Marketing)
Sustainability and overtourism policy (owned by Sustainable Tourism); leakage is treated here only as an economic-measurement idea

claims.claim: Tourism is not a single industry in standard national accounts; its contribution is measured with a satellite account (a Tourism/Travel and Tourism Satellite Account) that reallocates the portion of many industries' output bought by visitors, following the UN/UNWTO/OECD/Eurostat TSA:RMF 2008 framework so results are comparable with other economic statistics.
In 2023, U.S. travel and tourism's direct contribution (value added) was 3.03 percent of GDP, about $840 billion; the share was 3.04 percent in 2019 and dropped to 2.15 percent in 2020.
U.S. direct tourism employment was about 6.454 million jobs in 2023, an increase of 613,000 jobs over 2022 (which itself rose 734,000).

BEA estimates that in 2023 every dollar of direct tourism output required an additional 73 cents of indirect tourism output, and every 100 jobs supported directly required an additional 55 indirect tourism jobs.

In 2023, 325.5 million national-park visitors spent $26.4 billion in nearby gateway communities, which the NPS/USGS Visitor Spending Effects model estimates supported $55.6 billion in total U.S. economic output and 415,400 jobs (an implied output multiplier of about 2.1); lodging and restaurants had the largest direct contributions.

In the U.S. international accounts, spending by foreign visitors inside the United States is recorded as a services export under 'travel'; U.S. travel exports increased $38.3 billion in 2023 (travel imports increased $34.5 billion).

Economic leakage is the share of tourism revenue that leaves the destination economy, mainly through imports and non-local ownership; UNCTAD/UNEP estimates put average import-related leakage at roughly 40-50 percent of gross tourism earnings for small developing economies and 10-20 percent for advanced, diversified economies.

Leisure and hospitality is among the lowest-paying U.S. private supersectors: in December 2024 employer compensation averaged $19.90 per hour worked ($16.25 in wages and salaries), versus $44.67 ($31.47 in wages and salaries) for all private-industry workers.

Tourism multiplier estimates vary with the modeling method (input-output vs. computable general equilibrium), the size of the region studied, and how much spending leaks out, so a single 'the multiplier' figure should be treated as an estimate, not a constant.
Tourism spending is concentrated in the leisure and hospitality supersector (accommodation and food services plus arts, entertainment, and recreation), a sector marked by seasonal demand.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How large the tourism multiplier is
positions: Input-output models for developed, diversified economies (e.g., NPS/USGS for U.S. gateway communities) yield output multipliers around 2, because most supply chains are local.
Small or import-dependent economies show much lower effective multipliers because leakage removes a large share of each dollar before it recirculates.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Report multipliers as method- and place-specific estimates. The lesson uses BEA's direct-vs-indirect ratios and the NPS implied multiplier as concrete, dated U.S. examples and states plainly that the number varies with leakage and modeling choices.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept... introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') with no tourism-economics content; nothing in it was usable as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with sourced, dated figures for GDP share, employment, indirect ratios, exports, leakage, and wages.
Added the satellite-account rationale (tourism is not one industry) that the draft omitted entirely.
rightsIssues: UN Tourism (TSA:RMF) and UN Atlas of the Oceans/UNEP pages are copyrighted intergovernmental publications: REFERENCE_ONLY, facts synthesized and rewritten, no wording reproduced.
UNCTAD/UNEP leakage percentages are widely cited estimates from the early 2000s; presented as attributed, order-of-magnitude figures, not current-year data.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. Travel and Tourism Satellite Account for 2018–2023 (Survey of Current Business, Feb 2025)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary U.S. source. Read via WebFetch. Supports: tourism share of GDP 3.03% ($840B) in 2023 (3.04% 2019, 2.15% 2020); direct tourism employment 6.454M jobs in 2023 (+613,000); real direct tourism output $1.232T (+7.0%); every $1 direct output required $0.73 indirect output, every 100 direct jobs required 55 indirect jobs. U.S. government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: National Parks Contributed Record High $55.6 Billion to U.S. Economy, Supported 415,000 Jobs in 2023
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Reports NPS/USGS Visitor Spending Effects for 2023: 325.5M visitors, $26.4B direct spending in gateway communities, $55.6B total economic output, 415,400 jobs, $19.4B labor income; lodging $9.9B/89,200 jobs and restaurants $5.2B/68,600 jobs led direct contributions. Used for the worked multiplier example (implied output multiplier 55.6/26.4 = 2.11). Public domain.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, December and Annual 2023
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports: 'travel' is a services export/import in the international accounts covering goods and services acquired by travelers abroad (lodging, meals, local transport, entertainment); travel exports increased $38.3B and travel imports increased $34.5B in 2023. Used for the balance-of-payments framing. Public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Tourism Satellite Account: Recommended Methodological Framework 2008 (TSA:RMF 2008)
sourceRecords.provider: United Nations, UN Tourism (UNWTO), OECD, and Eurostat
sourceRecords.notes: PDF confirmed reachable (HTTP 200, application/pdf, unstats.un.org). Content summarized from BEA/UN Tourism descriptions and the official abstract: the TSA is the international standard for measuring tourism's economic contribution, built on the System of National Accounts, producing Tourism Direct GDP comparable across countries; noted by the UN Statistical Commission at its 39th session (Feb 2008). REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Negative Impacts: Leakage (Economic Impacts of Tourism)
sourceRecords.provider: UN Atlas of the Oceans (drawing on UNEP)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the leakage concept and cites UNCTAD estimates: average import-related leakage roughly 40-50% of gross tourism earnings for small developing economies and 10-20% for advanced diversified economies; the often-quoted figure that ~$5 of each $100 spent by a developed-country tourist stays in a developing destination. Early-2000s UNEP/UNCTAD estimates; presented as attributed and order-of-magnitude. REFERENCE_ONLY.
